# dsh-plugin-update

> [!WARNING]
> **Deprecated — this plugin is no longer maintained.**
> The latest official release o

f DeepSeek Harness already ships built-in
> plugin update checking, so this plugin is no longer need

ed. Please use the
> official feature instead of installing this plugin. This repository is kept
> f
or historical reference only; no further releases or fixes are planned.
English | 中文
A DeepSeek Harness bundle that answers "is there a newer version of my plugin?" and updates it in on
e click — from the plugin's own detail page.
## The problem it solves
A plugin installed into a DSH profile from npm stays at whatever version `pnpm` resolved the day it
was added. Nothing in the Web UI tells you a newer version exists:
- the **Plugins** page offers *Update* only for the Official catalog entries the installation ships;

- `list_bundles` reports the installed version and the saved spec, never the published one;
- `inst
all_bundle` refuses a package that is already installed (`already-installed`), so an update is alway
s *remove, then install*.
That sequence is easy to get wrong by hand and easy to forget. This bundle performs it for you.
## What it adds
Nothing in the sidebar. It contributes to the Plugins page's detail view, so the controls sit next t
o the ones the page already draws:
| Where | What |

| Detail page head | **Check for updates** beside the bundle's own switch and uninstall |
| Beside t

he title | **New version 4.10.0**, when a newer one exists |
| Under the page content | Installed →
newest, the source that answered, and the reason when a check fails or the newest version needs a ne
he source that answered, and the reason when a check fails or the newest version needs a newer DSH |
It answers for every source that has a remote to ask:
- **npm** — the registry document's `latest` tag, through the same registries the profile's plugin m
anager uses, in the same order. A profile behind `registry.npmmirror.com` is checked against the mir

ror rather than npmjs.
- **Git** — the `version` in the repository's `package.json`, read from the d
efault branch. `github:`, `gitlab:`, `bitbucket:`, `git+https://`, and `git@host:owner/repo` all res
olve. A Git dependency names a branch rather than a version, so an update reinstalls the same spec a
nd lets the branch supply the new code.
A local link, a tarball, or an alias has no remote to compare against, so the page says so instead o
f offering a button that cannot work. A Git address on a host with no readable raw file (a self-host
ed server) is reported the same way.
Each bundle's check falls into five states:
- **update** — a newer version exists and `engines.dsh` (else the `@deepseek-ai/dsh` peer range) adm

its the running DSH version.
- **incompatible** — a newer version exists but requires a DSH this pro

file does not run. The requirement and its source are shown; no update button appears.
- **current**

— the installed version is the newest one.
- **error** — the remote could not be read (offline, 404

, a malformed document). The reason is shown, and **Check for updates** retries.
- **unsupported** —
the dependency is a local link, a tarball, an alias, or a Git host this bundle cannot read. These a
s a local link, a tarball, an alias, or a Git host this bundle cannot read. These are never touched.
Checking one page asks only that package: the other sources come from a ten-minute cache.
## How an update runs
The Host half calls the profile's own `pluginManager` service, exactly as the Plugins page and the `
plugin_manager` tool do:

1. `removeBundle(name)` — deselects the bundle, unloads its rows, and runs `pnpm remove`.
2. `instal
lBundle(spec, { enabled, registry })` — installs the new version and reselects the bundle. `enabled`

preserves a bundle the person had switched off.
3. If step 2 fails, the previous spec is installed
again, so a failed update does not leave the plugin missing.
The saved spec keeps the range operator the dependency already used: `^4.8.1` becomes `^4.10.0`, not
`4.10.0`. A profile that pinned an exact version stays pinned. A Git dependency keeps its Git addre
ss, since a version pin would freeze the branch.
A Git update re-clones the repository, so it checks the host is reachable **before** removing anythi
ng. The plugin manager runs `git` with the environment it inherited and adds no proxy of its own; if
the host is only reachable through a proxy that `git` does not see, the install would fail after th
e removal had already happened. The check uses the same no-proxy conditions, so such a host is refus
ed while the plugin stays installed.
With HMR enabled, the replacement applies without a restart; a bundle that was running since startup
reports `restart-required`, and the page says so.
The bundle refuses to update itself: removing it would unload the routes answering the request.
Two side effects come from the plugin manager, not from this bundle, and they are the same ones the
shipped Update performs:
- The reinstalled bundle joins the **end** of `dsh.profile.bundles`. That order is configuration pre

cedence, so a profile where two bundles override the same row sees the updated one win afterwards.
-
A failed or cancelled installation after the removal leaves the package uninstalled; that is why th
e previous spec is installed again on failure, and why a Git host is proved reachable first.
## Configuration
None. The plugin manager's own `registry` and `fallbackRegistries` decide which registries are asked
. Git manifests are read over HTTPS; when `HTTPS_PROXY`/`HTTP_PROXY` is set, or the Windows per-user
proxy is configured, that proxy is used for those reads.
## HTTP surface
The Client half talks to the Host over three routes, because a plain-JS bundle cannot generate a `@R
alks to the Host over three routes, because a plain-JS bundle cannot generate a `@Remote` namespace:
[代码示例省略，未执行]
Mutations require the `x-plugin-update: 1` header, which a cross-site form cannot set and a cross-or
igin `fetch` cannot send without a CORS preflight these exact routes never answer.
